newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK govt debt repayment to slow M4 growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK govt debt repayment to slow M4 growth.

text.p: UK M4 money supply growth is expected to ease to 9.7 percent in the year to October, but could fall further because of a massive government debt repayment last month, analysts said.
A Reuter poll of economists, conducted late last week, showed a consensus expected a 0.5 percent increase in M4 in October, giving year-on-year growth of 9.7 percent, down from 9.9 in September.
But that poll was taken before official data released today showed a 4.4 billion stg public sector debt repayment in October
Economists had forecast a PSDR of around two billion.
"That makes quite a lot of difference to M4 forecasts," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

He, like the consensus, had forecast a 0.5 percent monthly increase in M4 but said that would probably now be lower. "It significantly increases the chances of M4 dropping nearer the government's monitoring range," he said.
The government has a three-to-nine percent monitoring range for annual broad money supply growth. It has rarely broken below the top of that range and in September was 9.9 percent.
The figures will be released at 0930 GMT on Wednesday.

Loynes also noted M4 rose 0.7 percent in October last year. That figure will now drop out of the year-on-year equation. "Any increase below that this month, will cut the annual rate." Conversely, weaker M4 growth in October is forecast to be matched by a pick-up in M4 lending to the private sector.
September M4 lending was surprisingly weak at 3.7 billion stg. For October, economists expect an increase of 4.9 billion.

"Given the background of above-trend growth, a recovery in the manufacturing sector and the continued housing market rebound, we do not believe last month's figures herald the start of a trend," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.
A hefty jump in M4 lending would go at least some way to offset the effect of October's massive government debt repayment on the overall M4 figure, analysts said.
But if lending failed to rebound, it could suggest a genuine slowdown in bank credit could be under way, Loynes said.

Figures from the Building Societies Association, due at the the same time as the M4 data on Wednesday, are forecast to show net new mortgage commitments worth 4.2 billion stg were approved in October. In September, approvals totalled 3.7 billion stg.
Darshini David, Loynes' fellow economist at HSBC Markets, said she expected 53,000 net new mortgage approvals in October, 1,000 more than in September.
September's figure confirmed "that mortgage demand continues to display robust growth as the housing market recovery strengthens," she said. "We expect this to continue in October."
One cautionary note for the housing market was the surprise quarter-point interest rate rise imposed by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on October 30.
David said expectations of further rate increases before the general election, rather than the last rise itself, would dampen mortgage demand slightly in the new year. Elections are due by May 1997.
